title: Why You Get The Interview But Not The Job (And How To Fix It)
description:
Interviews But No Offers? | The Real Reason You Get Rejected


You keep getting the interviews, and then a week later the rejection email lands. It's rarely your experience, your CV already proved that, and that's why you got the interview in the first place. In this video I break down the real reason you get interviews but no offers, and the 3 shifts that turn a final round interview into an actual job offer.

A company's interview process comes in 2 halves. The early rounds screen whether you can do the job. The final interview is almost always about positioning and trust, whether they can actually picture working with you, and that is where most candidates lose the offer. This is how to win it.


What you'll learn in this video:
- Why you keep getting interviews but no job offers, and why it has almost nothing to do with your experience
- Why a company's interview process comes in 2 halves, and why the final interview is decided on trust, not skill
- The difference between reciting and storytelling in a job interview, and why storytelling is what wins offers
- How to answer behavioural interview questions with a simple story structure, and why you lead with the result
- How to answer "why do you want to work here" so you do not sound like every other candidate


VIDEO CHAPTERS:
0:00 Interviews but no offers
0:37 The one thing Elamaran changed
0:49 Why interview processes come in 2 halves
1:33 The final interview is about trust, not skill
2:31 Shift 1: Stop reciting, start telling stories
3:41 Lead with the result
4:31 Shift 2: The 4 things they actually judge
5:14 The answer that wins on culture fit
6:14 Shift 3: The delivery they remember
8:32 What to do before your next interview


Stop preparing for the interview like it is an exam and start preparing to build trust. Here is how I can help:

WORK WITH ME:
The Offer Accelerator is my full system for landing offers faster. Personal brand, CV, LinkedIn, networking, applications, interviews, the lot.
https://community.offeraccelerator.co.uk/join?invitation_token=f1eaf2eb4891316c06b827f77255cb8b209dd952-daae48f6-0b4f-44fe-833a-04e7c487467c&utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=description&utm_campaign=interviews-but-no-offers


CONNECT WITH ME
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/olivercordingley
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/olivercordingley


WATCH NEXT:
The Interview Question That Costs You The Job


ABOUT ME:
I dropped out of university at 19 to build recruitment software and ATS systems used by hiring teams. For years I spoke to hundreds of hiring managers and recruiters every day, learning exactly how candidates get filtered, shortlisted, and hired from the inside. I started coaching friends through their job search using what I'd seen, then raised investment, built a software company, and hired my own team. I've seen hiring from every angle.

Today I help job seekers land offers faster using a proven 3-step system. I've coached hundreds of candidates into roles at firms like JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs, Deloitte, EY, and PwC and many more.

He was the same background that got him into the room in the first place. And then what he did is he changed one thing about the way he answered, and then that fourth interview turned into that offer and a job that almost doubled his salary from 27,500 to 58,000 pounds. So, if you keep getting those interviews and then a week later the rejection email lands, you need to watch this because the reason you're not getting that offer has almost nothing to do with your experience. So, a company's interview process comes in two halves. So, the first few rounds, the online test, you know, the numerical reasonings, that first technical interview, they're all there to check one thing. And it's basically, can you do the job? skill screen and it's tangible and it's about ability and and competency. And it's basically a pass or fail. But here's the part that almost nobody realizes. By the time that you reach that final stage interview, you've already passed all of that. So, if you're four or five rounds deep, think about how much time that whole team has already put into you. They decided that you're good enough on paper. They've qualified your ability. So, that final interview is almost never about whether you can actually do the job. It's purely an emotional decision. And the real question in the room is, can I actually work with this person, you know, 40 hours a week for the next few years? And that's the exact bit that you keep losing on. So, it's not your ability, it's your positioning and it's the trust that you build in that interview room. Because most candidates they walk into that final interview still just trying to prove that they're competent when when competence was settled, you know, two or three rounds ago. And what they do is they keep showing up as a candidate and then the offer goes to the person who shows up like a colleague. So, you need to think about it from the other side of the table. So, the employer they've probably got three or four people left who, you know, they can all do the job. And on paper, there's barely anything different between them. So, it doesn't really come down to who's the most qualified. It comes down to who they trust and who they've warmed to and who they actually picture on their team. So, when you recite your interview answers, none of that lands and when you tell a story, all of it does. So, let me show you the three shifts that turn that final round interview from a rejection into an offer. And every one of them is really about the same thing. It's building that trust and getting them to see you as a colleague instead of a candidate. So, let's start with the first because this one is where most people go wrong. So, the first shift is you need to stop reciting and you need to start telling stories. Now, here's what reciting actually sounds like. You know, someone asked you to tell them a time about when you, you know, solved a problem and then you go into this polished paragraph, probably using the STAR or CAR method, that you've clearly said out loud, probably 40 times in the mirror before that interview. And probably on paper, it's probably word perfect, but it's completely forgettable. So, then the interviewer's attention just drifts off somewhere and then they're probably just waiting for you to stop. Whereas a story is a completely different thing. A story has a scene, a problem, what you actually did and how it turned out. And it's the exact same shape that you, you know, when you tell a story to your friends or your family or around dinner, for example. You set the scene, something goes wrong, you deal with it and then there's something that happened. You don't need a fancy method or some five-letter acronym for this. You just need to talk like a human being who was actually there. And before we even get into the story, watch how you start it. Because most people, what they do is they spend the first 30 seconds explaining the company, the team, the whole background before they even get anywhere near the actual situation. And by the time they reach that point, the interviewer's attention's gone. So, set the scene in a sentence or two and then get straight into the meat of your answer. And here's the one tweak that also makes a massive difference. You need to lead with the result. So, most candidates who come to me after they've been rejected, what they do is they save the outcome to the very end. So, then the interviewer has to sit through two minutes of build-up before they find out why the story even mattered. So, what you need to do is flip it on its head. So, a candidate that I worked with used to bury his first number right at the end of every answer. And what we did is we changed it, and he started opening with something like this. I made a change that saved business around 4 million, and here's how I did it. Now, the interviewer is leaning in for the whole story instead of just waiting around for the whole point. So, they're not just hiring on skill set. What they're doing is they're choosing someone that they've got to sit next to every day for the next few years. That's what they're preparing to do. "Oh, I love what you do. I'm really passionate about the industry." It tells them nothing, and it sounds exactly like every other candidate on that day. So, the fix is to get specific and make it personal. So, what you need to do is reference one real thing about them, and then say why it actually matters to you. What they remember is the feeling that they left with. Like, did this person feel sharp or warm or, you know, easy to work with? And that feeling is what walks into the room when they sit down and they decide as a committee. And you could be the most qualified person in the process and still lose on that feeling. And this matters even more on a video interview because you have to remember your energy just gets flattened through a screen. So, that thing that feels like normal enthusiasm to you comes across as a bit flat on camera. So, you actually have to put in a bit more into it that feels natural and just to make it land more normally. Now, here's where most people sabotage their own delivery. What they do, and I see it time and time again, they memorize their answers word for word. And memorizing is the most fragile thing you can do because the second that you get a question in a slightly different shape than you practiced, the whole script falls apart and then you freeze. And the fix isn't just to memorize harder, it's to stop writing your answers out. And you need to start saying them out loud. And then the words come out fresh and you feel comfortable about it. Then what you do is you rehearse the structure. So, you don't rehearse the exact words. Now, if you're nervous in the interview, you're honestly allowed to just say it. Something like, "I'll be honest with you. I'm a little bit nervous because I really want this one." And a decent interviewer warms to that straight away because it's honest and it tells them that you care. And it also it will calm you down because you've already said it out loud. Because the reality is the nerves in the interview room are never the problem. It's always just trying to hide it because it builds pressure on you and then you start to forget. So, going back to Elon Musk for a second, like nothing about his CV changed across those four final interviews. He started showing up like a future colleague. So, what he did is he told stories. He built trust and that interview turned into an offer that doubled his salary. And remember, he was exactly the same on paper. All of it changed just on how he communicated it. So, before your next interview, you need to do this. Take three or four of your best stories, the ones that you, you know, genuinely proud of, and then practice them out loud as stories, not scripts. Lead with the result, cut the second example, and prepare one real reason you want to work at that company. And ideally, from actually talking to someone who works there already. So, if you want the full breakdown of all of this, you know, the exact story structures, you know, the questions that catch people out, I'm going to go through all of this inside the Offer Accelerator and the link is in the description below if you want to join. And I promise you, if you get this right and you master storytelling, you're going to stop walking in as a candidate that they're judging and you're going to start walking in as a colleague that they really want and that is where you get the attractive offers.
